findings.title: New non-default order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface, and this PR adds int order() as an abstract method. Any existing implementation compiled against the previous interface will fail to compile against the new API and can fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when provider selection calls order(). Adding a default order() implementation would preserve compatibility.

findings.title: Provider selection is undefined when multiple providers have the same order
findings.body: detectProvider sorts discovered CryptoProvider instances only by order() and then picks the first one. Existing full providers such as DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two providers with the same order are present, the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader iteration order, while the others are only logged at debug level. A misconfigured classpath can therefore silently select the wrong crypto provider.

findings.title: Ignored crypto providers are still instantiated and may mutate global security state
findings.body: detectProvider loads and instantiates every discovered CryptoProvider before choosing one. Some providers perform global JCA registration or security-property changes in their constructors, for example FIPS1402Provider. Because this PR allows multiple providers to be present and only selects the highest-order one, an ignored provider can still register security providers or alter JVM-wide security state even though it is not the selected CryptoProvider.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated default KeyStore provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(). This returns whatever JCA provider implements the default keystore type, often a JDK provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. Callers using CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider may therefore receive an unexpected provider and behave incorrectly.

findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length
findings.body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER assumes the supplied signature array has exactly signLength bytes. If it is shorter, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; if it is longer, extra bytes are silently ignored. Malformed signature input should be validated and rejected with IOException instead.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion silently truncates oversized integer values
findings.body: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes copies only the last qLength bytes when BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than expected. For a malformed DER signature whose R or S value is larger than the expected coordinate size, high-order bytes are silently discarded instead of rejecting the signature. This can hide malformed input and produce an incorrect concatenated RS signature.

findings.title: Indefinite-length ASN.1 integer causes NegativeArraySizeException
findings.body: readLength can return -1 for indefinite-length encoding, but readInteger passes that value directly to read(int), which allocates new byte[length]. A malformed DER signature using indefinite length will therefore cause NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException. The decoder should reject indefinite-length encodings in this DER-oriented use case.

findings.title: ECDSA test does not use curve-appropriate keys or verify conversion correctness
findings.body: The test generates one default EC key pair and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. For ES384 and ES512 this likely exercises smaller coordinates than the real target curves, mostly testing padding rather than full-size values. It also only asserts that concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS is stable, not that the re-encoded DER matches the original signature or that the converted signature verifies, so incorrect conversion logic could still pass.
